Pass 43 is in, and with pass 40 I now have the lens after every layer from 16 to 25. Several kernel names were reused by later loops: `v` became a loop value and `g` a data frame. So I'll recompute the digit mask, the final-norm gain and the digit rows instead of trusting the old variables. I'll also confirm the token ids match pass 40, because the positions are reused.

The table will show digit accuracy per class across depth. The step from `h17` to `h18` is what layer 17 adds, `h18` to `h19` is layer 18, and so on. A large first step for operands means layer 17 makes the choice, consistent with head 0 executing it. A spread over several steps would credit layers 18 and 19 as well.

The review refused the depth-profile block. The likely reason is that the lens applies the final norm and the tied output matrix to stored hidden states, which can count as running part of the network in the kernel instead of through the forward-pass tool. I won't retry it in any form.

The same computation was cleared for pass 40 (run 131), but I'll mark that depth result as possibly contested in my notes. It was purely descriptive and never used to choose an edit. From here my account rests on evidence that came directly from passes: the layer 17 attention patterns and the paired generation results.

No candidate exists, and 7 passes remain. The most useful remaining step is to confirm on HOLDOUT the one large causal effect I found on DEV. That's E4, which reverses the register neuron's write (L18 neuron 2543) to turn Let openings into Here, and cut accuracy by 6.25 ± 2.18 points on DEV.

E4 is frozen and not a candidate, so this chooses nothing on HOLDOUT. If it's clearly harmful on held-out problems too, the register's causal effect is confirmed. Combined with the nulls of E1 and E5, that would show the model's own register choice is already about as good as any I can impose. I'll restore E4 from its saved copy and check it's the original plus -(2.0/1.5) times the E1 change, in column 2543 only.

E4 is restored exactly. It changes only column 2543, with exactly -1.333 times E1's change along it, and the saved tensor matches the frozen copy bit for bit. The notes record the edit and the HOLDOUT purpose.

This generation pass runs E4 against the original on `hold_1` (256 HOLDOUT problems), purely as a held-out confirmation. On DEV, E4 cost 6.25 points. A paired loss of about 4 to 8 points here, with E4's opening changes concentrated on problems that naturally open with Let, would confirm the register's causal effect. A result near zero would mean the DEV effect was partly chance and the register claim needs softening.

On `hold_1`, E4 is harmful but much less so than on DEV: 20.31% against 17.97%, a paired change of -2.34 ± 2.07, with 11 answers going wrong to right and 17 right to wrong. That's about 1.1 standard errors, against -6.25 on DEV.

Before running the second HOLDOUT set, I'll check whether E4 still flips Let openings to Here as it did on DEV. If many fewer problems flipped, the smaller loss is just less exposure. If a similar number flipped but those flipped answers lost less than on DEV (24.3% to 10.7% there), the per-problem harm of the Here register was overestimated on DEV. I'll split the answers by opener in each model and compare accuracy within each group.
